Alphonso Smith Jr. had a good run with the Detroit Lions

Alphonso Smith Jr., the former Detroit Lions’ star player, has passed away tragically at his home in Florida after staying out of the spotlight for the last decade. Hours before his death, Alphonso Smith Jr. made a concerning post on Facebook which has hinted that he might have had committed suicide. While things remain unconfirmed, the news of his death has taken a turn.As per reports, back in 2015, Alphonso Smith Jr. was working as a head coach at Pahokee High School after retiring from the league.But the then 29 year old was removed from his position amid controversial allegations of "inappropriate conduct” which even led to an investigation by a local sheriff’s office.Not a lot of details have been made public about the situation but Alphonso Smith Jr. has hinted at it in his apparent suicide note.While the former Detroit Lions did speak about "fighting" demons, he also wrote, “To my family, BABY, my MOM, my siblings, things happened to your boy, your brother while I was little that an older lady did onto me…”The 40 year old added, “As a result guys, I did the same onto others! I have HURT so many! I needed help & did not get it!”Alphonso Smith Jr.’s death has sparked chaos among fans as many are shocked by it as many sympathised with his situation.A fan posted, “He wrote that he was abused as a kid and that he later hurt other people. Both of those things can be true, and neither one makes suicide the answer. Families on every side of this deserve space, not a comment-section verdict.”Another fan wrote, “So sad that people internalize abuse and do the same to others… disgusting, inexcusable shit he did, but it’s just sad to see how these cycles continue smfh.”A third fan posted, “This is heartbreaking. 💔 You never really know what someone is battling behind closed doors. Praying for his family, friends, and everyone who loved him. May Alphonso Smith Jr. rest in peace”.To make matters worse, Alphonso Smith Jr. landed in legal trouble and faced a misdemeanor battery charge in Palm Beach County after an alleged altercation with his ex girlfriend in 2016.Back in 2012, Alphonso Smith Jr. was released by the Detroit Lions.Later, he was brought back for another season as Alphonso Smith Jr. ended his career in the league recording 88 tackles with 19 pass deflections, eight interceptions, two defensive touchdowns, two forced fumbles, and two fumble recoveries.Alphonso Smith Jr.’s family has stayed out of the spotlight and has not opened up about his tragic death yet.

Article Title: Inspiring story on leadership: "I always define leadership as: do you care about your teammates...and do you care what we're trying to accomplish"- How Tom Brady led teams to greatness
Article Text:
Tom Brady (Getty Images)

Tom Brady’s leadership philosophy was built around caring

PBD Podcast

2023

“Tom Brady on the Art of Leading Teammates,”

When and where Tom Brady shared the leadership message

caring about the other person and collectively caring about what the group was trying to achieve

Tom Brady learned team-first leadership at Michigan

University of Michigan

How Brady put his leadership philosophy into practice

Tom Brady spent more than two decades being judged by rings, records and unforgettable performances. Yet when he talks about leadership, his definition reaches far beyond statistics. In a discussion about motivating teammates, Brady explained why genuine care, trust and a shared purpose shaped the way he led. His words offer a revealing look at the mindset behind one of football's most successful careers.Brady's approach to leadership was not simply about demanding more from the players around him. He believed a leader first had to build a relationship with the people he expected to follow him.During the, Brady discussed his leadership style and what helped him motivate teammates. The conversation, published in, turned toward leadership, when host Patrick Bet-David asked Brady about the methods he used to drive his players.Brady's answer centered on one word: caring.He explained that the relationship between a leader and teammates cannot be purely transactional. Players need to believe that the person beside them genuinely cares about them and about the goal they are pursuing together.That idea also appears in Brady's later Harvard Business Review work, where he expanded on his definition of team leadership. The article,was published in 2024 and explored seven principles he believed helped leaders bring out the best in teammates.The quote at the center of this discussion captures that philosophy:“I always define leadership as, do you care about your teammates or coworkers, and do you care what we’re trying to accomplish?” Brady. “That, to me, is great leadership. And there are a lot of people that go about those in different ways.”The wording is powerful because Brady does not begin with authority, experience or talent. He begins with people.For him, leadership starts with asking whether teammates know they matter and whether everyone remains committed to the same objective.The quote has circulated online in shortened form, but its underlying idea is supported by Brady's own extended comments.In the 2023 PBD Podcast conversation, Brady said his view of relationships in a team environment came down to. He argued that trust develops when people know their leader genuinely cares about them.That conversation gives important context to the quote. Brady was not describing leadership as a motivational speech or a title attached to a job. He was talking about the daily relationship between teammates.He also stressed the importance of vulnerability and mutual trust. In his view, players had to feel comfortable relying on one another. That trust could not be manufactured simply because someone was the quarterback or captain.Brady's later HBR article developed the same philosophy in greater detail. He wrote that leadership comes down to caring about teammates and caring about winning together. He connected that belief to trust, arguing that people are more willing to give their best when they feel valued by those around them.Brady traced much of his team-first mindset back to his time at theHis college career did not follow the straightforward path often associated with a future NFL superstar. He redshirted as a freshman and later found himself behind other quarterbacks on the depth chart. Yet those setbacks became part of his leadership education.In his HBR article, Brady recalled competing with Brian Griese for the starting quarterback position. Griese won the job, and Brady said his role was to support and challenge him in practice rather than undermine him. Michigan went undefeated that season and won the national championship.That experience reinforced a lesson that stayed with him.Individual recognition was not the ultimate prize. Winning as a group mattered more.Brady later described this mindset through an old sports question: whether someone wants to be a star or a champion. For him, the answer was clear. He wanted to contribute to something bigger than himself.That attitude became especially important during his NFL career. As a quarterback, Brady naturally occupied one of the most visible positions on the field. Every touchdown, mistake and major decision could draw attention to him.But he repeatedly emphasized the people around him.Brady's definition of leadership becomes more meaningful when paired with the examples he gave from his playing career.At Tampa Bay, he noticed that screen plays were producing poor results because offensive linemen were missing blocks. Rather than simply criticizing them, Brady created his own incentive. He promised to pay each offensive lineman $1,000 whenever a screen play gained more than 15 yards.The money was not necessarily the main point. Brady believed the gesture showed appreciation and made the linemen feel involved in the outcome.He also spoke about recognizing people whose contributions were less visible. Football teams rely on trainers, equipment staff, meal workers and many others whose names rarely appear in headlines.Brady believed leaders should make those people feel valued too.His approach also involved holding teammates accountable. Because he worked to establish trust, he felt he could challenge players directly without making them feel personally attacked. That balance between support and honesty became another important part of his leadership style.Perhaps that is what makes Brady's words resonate beyond football.A quarterback can throw a perfect pass, but he cannot win alone. A business executive can set a strategy, but employees still have to believe in it. A coach can design a game plan, but players have to trust one another enough to execute it.Brady's message is therefore much bigger than his NFL career.Leadership, in his view, is not about standing above everyone else. It is about standing with them, understanding what they need and making sure everyone remains connected to the same goal.That is why his simple question carries so much weight: Do you care about your teammates, and do you care about what you are trying to accomplish together?For a player who spent his career chasing championships, Brady's answer offers a different definition of what it means to win. The scoreboard may measure the final result, but the relationships built along the way can determine whether a team ever gets there in the first place.
Article Summary: Quarterback tom brady's leadership philosophy was built around caring. Brady said a leader first had to build a relationship with the people he expected to follow him. Brady traced his team-first mindset back to his time at the university of michigan.

Article Title: He started playing at three-and-a-half; two decades later, reached the highest-ever T20I rating: How Abhishek Sharma conquered the fastest format
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma (AFP Photo)

The boy who started cricket at three-and-a-half

Yuvraj Singh's influence shapes his fearless approach

From breakthrough star to world-record holder

A T20 batter built for destruction

T20I career so far

Abhishek Sharma has come a long way from the little boy in Amritsar who first picked up a cricket bat at the age of three-and-a-half. On his birthday, his journey stands out as one of the most remarkable rises in modern T20 cricket, from a promising youngster in Punjab to an India regular and the holder of the highest-ever ICC T20I batting rating.Abhishek's father, Raj Kumar Sharma, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game when he was just three-and-a-half. The youngster quickly developed an obsession with batting and progressed through Punjab's age-group system.His numbers soon began attracting attention. During the 2015-16 Vijay Merchant Trophy, Abhishek scored more than 1,200 runs at an average of 109.09 and also claimed 57 wickets. He captained Punjab to the Under-19 Asia Cup title in 2016 before becoming part of India's victorious Under-19 World Cup campaign in 2018.The IPL came at just 17, when Delhi Daredevils picked him in the 2018 auction. His career, however, did not explode immediately. Abhishek spent several seasons developing his game through domestic cricket and the IPL before finding the perfect platform for his aggressive style.A major influence during that period was Yuvraj Singh. The former India all-rounder became Abhishek's mentor and worked closely with him, particularly during the Covid-19 lockdown.Yuvraj understood the youngster's attacking instincts and encouraged him to embrace them rather than become overly cautious. That philosophy eventually became the foundation of Abhishek's T20 game.His international breakthrough came after making his T20I debut in July 2024. In February 2025, Abhishek produced one of the most devastating T20I innings by an Indian batter when he smashed 135 off just 54 balls against England in Mumbai. The innings contained 13 sixes and a 37-ball century, announcing him as one of India's most dangerous T20 batters.The 135 was only the beginning. During the 2025 Asia Cup, Abhishek established himself as India's attacking force at the top of the order. He scored 314 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of 200 and was named Player of the Tournament as India won the competition.His performances pushed him to the top of the ICC T20I batting rankings and eventually into record-breaking territory. After scoring 61 against Sri Lanka, Abhishek reached 931 rating points, the highest-ever rating achieved by a men's T20I batter.He surpassed Dawid Malan's previous record of 919 and moved beyond the best ratings achieved by India's Suryakumar Yadav and Virat Kohli.The numbers behind Abhishek's rise were extraordinary. In 2025, he became the first player to score more than 1,000 runs in T20 cricket in a calendar year while maintaining a strike rate above 200. He finished the year at a strike rate of 202 and smashed 108 sixes.His IPL performances were equally destructive. Playing for Sunrisers Hyderabad, Abhishek produced a stunning 141 off 55 balls against Punjab Kings in IPL 2025. He reached his fifty in only 16 balls and his century in 40, hitting 14 fours and 10 sixes as Hyderabad chased down 246. The innings broke KL Rahul's record for the highest score by an Indian batter in IPL history.His development has been shaped by several influential figures. Apart from Yuvraj, Abhishek has drawn lessons from players such as Shikhar Dhawan, Brian Lara and Travis Head. At Sunrisers, his partnership with Head showed how effectively his aggressive approach could work against the best bowling attacks.At the 2026 T20 World Cup, Abhishek added another major achievement to his growing list, playing a crucial role in India's title-winning campaign, including a blistering 52 off 21 balls in the final against New Zealand.Abhishek Sharma has played 56 T20Is between 2024 and 2026, scoring 1,629 runs in 55 innings at an average of 30.73 and a remarkable strike rate of 187.24. He has registered two centuries and 11 fifties, with a highest score of 135. His aggressive approach is reflected in his boundary count, with the left-hander hitting 164 fours and 104 sixes in his international career so far.
Article Summary: Abhishek sharma started playing cricket at the age of three-and-a-half. His father, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game. His development has been shaped by influential mentor yuvraj singh. He is the holder of the highest-ever icc t20i batting rating. Abhishek sharma has played 56 t20is between 2024 and 2026.

NEW DELHI: Anshuman Hooda bursts into laughter when asked to choose between his office laptop and his cricket ball. “My cricket ball is my best friend,” he tells TimesofIndia.com.His elder brother, Vikram Hooda, says their mother, Prem Lata Singh, a primary class teacher at a Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) school, is happy to see Anshuman pursue cricket, especially now that he has a stable job. “Earlier, they used to say that he needed a job. Now that he has one and is doing well, she is happy,” Vikram says of their parents.Anshuman had a breakout 2026 Delhi Premier League (DPL) season -- emerging as the Purple Cap winner with 22 scalps -- which played a crucial role in South Delhi Superstarz's title triumph.But there was a time when Hooda thought cricket had run its course. Two attempts at the Under-23 trials had gone by without success. There was no age-group cricket on his résumé, no traditional pathway through Delhi's junior system and no obvious route into first-class cricket. He had an engineering degree from Delhi Technological University (DTU) and a job at EY. The sensible thing, he thought, was to move on.“I tried for Under-23 for two years, but I couldn’t make it. I thought it would be very difficult because I hadn’t played any professional cricket or age-group cricket.It would have been very difficult to directly get selected for the Ranji Trophy or first-class cricket,” Anshuman recollects.“So at that time, I thought I should quit cricket and pursue my career in engineering or something.”But just when he thought of walking away from the game, his coach Harish Dagar, who runs a cricket academy named Delhi Cricket Hub in Delhi's Paschim Vihar, and trains youngsters at DTU, stepped up.“It was in 2023. He had just graduated. He had got the job through campus placement and was ready to move on with his life. I pleaded with him to give it one more year. I asked him to come to my academy four days a week for a year, and if nothing would pan out, I would let him pursue his corporate job,” reminisces Dagar.Then came the Delhi Premier League (DPL). And with it came a completely different possibility. For a young man who had arrived late to leather-ball cricket, DPL became the stage on which his raw pace, athleticism and appetite for fast bowling could finally be seen. The numbers followed. The attention followed, and now Anshuman is finally ready to become a full-time cricketer.“I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament. So in the coming times, I might shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all,” he says.Anshuman is 25 and, in cricketing terminology, he can be called a late bloomer. But the most unusual thing about Anshuman's story is perhaps where it began. Not with a cricket academy. Not with a junior tournament. Not with a childhood obsession with bowling. With roller skates.Growing up, Anshuman was a national-level roller skater. Cricket existed around him, but it was not initially the sport that defined him. His elder brother Vikram had played cricket, and there was, as Anshuman puts it, a familiar sibling dynamic. His brother took science. He took science. His brother studied engineering. He studied engineering. But when it came to cricket, Anshuman's journey took its own route.It was only when he reached college that the game began to take hold.“I just started playing in college, and that’s when I got into leather-ball cricket professionally, playing for the college team and all. That’s when I fell in love with bowling fast, getting wickets and the aggression that comes with it. I just loved bowling fast.”That love became the starting point of something neither his résumé nor his previous sporting journey could have predicted.Harish Dagar first noticed Anshuman in 2019 while they were at university. What caught his eye was not a polished fast bowler. It was the physical package.Fitness. Arm speed. Natural movement.Anshuman was playing tennis-ball cricket when Dagar asked him to try medium pace. The first attempts were raw and erratic, but there was enough pace and athletic ability for the coach to believe there was something worth developing.“His body alignment was natural. His strength was natural, and his pace was natural. But he didn't have enough strength in his body initially. That's why I told him that if you don't maintain your fitness along with your natural pace, you will face problems," says Dagar.“He was also busy with his job. He couldn't always take proper sessions. He would come at night, then have to go to the gym and take practice sessions. It was very hectic.“I worked on his mind 80-85 per cent. I made him mentally strong. I told him never to think that he was tired or burdened.“Once I worked on his mindset and the roadmap was clear in front of him, he knew what he had to do. At one point he had to focus on fitness, at another he had to do his job, and then he had to come to me for his sessions."Anshuman graduated from DTU with a degree in Production and Industrial Engineering and joined a multinational company in 2023. He worked from home, which helped him juggle the demands of employment and an increasingly serious cricket career. But balancing the two was never going to be easy.Fast bowling is an unforgiving craft. It demands strength, recovery, repetition and hours of training. Dagar's approach was to build Anshuman patiently, focusing not merely on speed but on the physical and mental foundations that could allow him to bowl fast consistently.Anshuman also had to understand his own body. He had dealt with niggles and the physical toll that comes with repeatedly accelerating, landing and transferring his entire body weight through a bowling action.“Fast bowling is not a very comfortable activity for the body. You accelerate, then your whole body has to absorb the impact before you bowl. It definitely takes a toll on the body,” he says.But there was no great mystery behind his motivation. He adds: “It was just the love for the sport and the love for bowling fast that kept me motivated and helped me come back stronger every time.”That attitude has been central to his development.Dagar describes the next stage of the process in more professional terms: periodisation, rest, strength work, workload scheduling, diet, physiotherapy and technical skills. Anshuman had to develop a stock ball and variations such as the leg-cutter and off-cutter while ensuring that his body could cope with the demands of pace.The objective was never simply to produce a fast delivery. It was to produce a fast bowler. The first real crack in the wall came through the DPL.In 2024, he got his opportunity with South Delhi, initially finding chances hard to come by. Then came a spell that changed perceptions. The next season brought more opportunities, including a five-wicket haul, and soon IPL franchises were looking at him as a net bowler and trial candidate.The journey from someone contemplating quitting cricket to someone attracting franchise attention had happened remarkably quickly. For Anshuman, the attention became tangible when Shikhar Dhawan , the owner of his DPL team, spoke to him after his performances.“Shikhar Dhawan himself, the team owner, surprised me. He came and we had a little conversation. He gave me some very good tips and a direction to work towards from here,” he says.It was a moment of validation. For someone who had spent years outside the conventional cricket pathway, being noticed by an established name carried significance beyond a conversation.At 140 kmph, Anshuman possesses the one commodity that can change a fast bowler's career quickly: pace. Coach Dagar believes there is more to come. Anshuman is not shy about wanting it.“Definitely, speed is what I want. If I can, I will definitely look to bowl even faster and build the strength and skills to do that, while making sure there is no compromise on accuracy and line,” said Anshuman.That final clause is important. Pace can attract attention. Accuracy keeps a fast bowler in a team. For Anshuman, the next challenge is therefore not simply touching a bigger number on the speed gun. It is learning how to sustain high pace across long spells, particularly in red-ball cricket.He is already thinking about it. “These are the things we prepare for. Who bowls in a four-day or five-day game and bowls long spells with the same effort? That is what I am preparing for. If I get an opportunity, I will definitely do that.”Anshuman's ambition is clear. First, Delhi. Then first-class cricket. Then, eventually, IPL and India.“The eventual goal is to play and win matches for the country. That is my ultimate goal,” he says.There is, however, one more conversation happening in Anshuman's life. The conversation between security and possibility. An engineering degree and a job at a good company offer a predictable future. And he has got a promotion before the start of the DPL season as well. Cricket offers something very different: uncertainty, competition and the possibility of a career that can disappear as quickly as it arrives.For now, Anshuman has returned to work. But his cricket has progressed to the point where continuing to divide himself between the two may no longer be possible.“Currently, I have joined back. But as I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament, I might, in the coming times, shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all.”It is a significant sentence from someone who once thought about quitting the sport altogether. There is also a quiet irony in the fact that the engineer who learned to manage competing demands may soon have to choose one.Anshuman knows where he wants to go.“I will give it my all. Let’s see what happens ahead.”

Argentina began paying tribute to Lionel Messi after the football great announced his retirement from international football earlier this week.The first tribute came during the Copa Argentina match between Velez Sarsfield and Boca Juniors on Wednesday, when play was stopped in the 10th minute for a round of applause at the Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes.Fans across the stadium stood and applauded Messi, bringing the game to a halt for a brief moment.Two of Messi's former Argentina teammates, Leandro Paredes and Manuel Lanzini, were on the pitch during the tribute.The match later ended 0-0, with Boca Juniors winning the penalty shootout 4-3.The tribute follows a decision by the Argentine Football Association, which announced that referees will stop play in the 10th minute of every match in the upcoming round of the Clausura tournament, as well as in other men's and women's competitions across the country, to honour Messi's international career.Messi announced his international retirement after the 2026 FIFA World Cup, ending a career that lasted 21 years with the Argentina team.He finished with 125 goals and 68 assists in 207 appearances for Argentina.In his retirement message, Messi said the decision "hurts the depths of my soul", but added that he "knows the time has come" to stop representing his country.Messi's biggest achievement with Argentina came when he led the team to the 2022 FIFA World Cup title in Qatar.He also helped Argentina win the Copa America in 2021 and 2024, ending the country's 28-year wait for a major trophy.Although he is one of Argentina's biggest sporting icons, Messi has never played club football professionally in his home country. He moved to Barcelona at the age of 13 and built his career there.Messi has retired only from international football and continues to play club football for Inter Miami in Major League Soccer.

Article Title: 'Serving country against biological clock': Spain to fund egg freezing for women footballers; what does it mean?
Article Text:
Mariona Caldentey, Irene Paredes, Alexia Putellas, Claudia Pina and Olga Carmona look on during a training session at RCDE Stadium on June 02, 2025 in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo/Getty Images)

Players raised the issue with the federation

What egg freezing means for elite athletes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

No clear rules yet in women's football

Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers, in a move aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level.According to a report by EL Pais, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) is finalising an agreement with a fertility clinic that will allow members of the Spain women's team to undergo egg vitrification. The agreement is expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.The move comes as more women athletes face the challenge of fitting pregnancy into long sporting careers. A football career can continue into a player's thirties, but pregnancy often means several months away from training and competition, and returning to the highest level can be difficult.Former Spain captain Alexia Putellas said the team's captains had discussed the issue with the federation and welcomed the proposal."The federation understands that you are serving your country against your biological clock, that you cannot stop and cannot be a mother because you need your body to work," Putellas was quoted as saying by EL Pais."The group of captains had a concern because it is very important for a player to experience World Cups, but that means that those of us who have the desire to become mothers do not find it easy to fit it in."The federation has not yet confirmed whether it will cover the full treatment, only the egg preservation process, or also the egg retrieval procedure.Sports medicine specialist Eva Ferrer said egg vitrification has become a topic of discussion in women's football only over the past couple of years.She explained that there is still limited research on how ovarian stimulation affects athletes. "There are not enough studies on how the treatment [ovarian stimulation] could affect, for example, the joints or soft tissue," Ferrer said as quoted by EL Pais.She added that training may need to be adjusted during treatment to reduce the risk of injury. She also said the medications used during the process must be declared through a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) so athletes do not face anti-doping issues.The treatment usually lasts about two weeks. During that period, the player injects hormonal medication to stimulate the ovaries so multiple eggs mature instead of one. Doctors then retrieve the eggs through a procedure performed under sedation.After the procedure, players may experience bleeding, discomfort, swelling, fluid retention, migraines and lower energy levels while the ovaries recover. Clinics generally recommend collecting around 10 oocytes, though the process can be repeated if needed.Gynecologist Rebeca Beguería said elite athletes do not return to peak physical condition immediately after treatment."The medical protocol states that normal life can be resumed, but for a high-performance athlete these are days when you do not perform at the same level: you will not run as fast or at the same intensity," she told EL Pais.She added that players face a greater risk of injury and abdominal damage during recovery."Your body's blood is redistributed; it is concentrated there; the abdomen and chest are more swollen, there is a tendency to migraines and fluid retention."Beguería also pointed out that while egg freezing helps players delay pregnancy, it does not remove the medical risks associated with becoming pregnant at an older age."Medically, the recommendation is that women get pregnant as early as possible, because biologically we are designed to be mothers by, at most, age 35 and we have extended that."The proposal has also highlighted the lack of regulations around fertility treatment in professional women's football.Lawyer Tania Tejeira wrote in an opinion piece in Palco23 that neither FIFA nor UEFA currently has a specific protocol covering treatments such as egg freezing or other assisted reproductive technologies, despite more players choosing these options.At present, the main international guidance comes from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), which requires medications used during fertility treatment to be reviewed and, where necessary, approved through a Therapeutic Use Exemption.
Article Summary: Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers. The move is aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level. The agreement is expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.

Article Title: Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family
Article Text:
Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family

What did Andre Agassi mean when he said, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood”?

How did becoming a father change Agassi’s view of his own childhood?

How did Steffi Graf fit into Agassi’s approach to raising their children?

What does Agassi’s quote tell us about his idea of parenthood?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Andre Agassi’s words, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” offer a deeply personal look at how becoming a parent changed the tennis legend’s view of his own life. Agassi grew up in a world where tennis was not simply a sport but a major part of his everyday life, with intense training and expectations starting at a very young age. Years later, after becoming one of tennis’ biggest stars, he and his wife, fellow tennis legend Steffi Graf, built a family life around their two children, Jaden and Jaz. For Agassi, watching his children grow gave him the chance to experience some of the simple moments of childhood that he felt he had missed himself.The quote is closely connected to Agassi’s own experience growing up. He started playing tennis as a young child and was pushed toward the sport by his father, Mike Agassi. His father had a clear dream for him: he wanted his son to become one of the best tennis players in the world.That dream eventually came true.Agassi went on to become world No. 1 and won eight Grand Slam singles titles during his career. But reaching that level meant spending much of his childhood training, competing and preparing for professional tennis.For a young child, that kind of life can leave little room for ordinary experiences. Instead of having complete freedom to decide how he wanted to spend his time, Agassi’s days were largely connected to tennis.That is where his famous quote becomes especially powerful.When he says he “gave up” his childhood, he is looking back at the years he spent becoming a professional athlete. But he is also talking about what those sacrifices eventually allowed him to do.His success gave him the freedom to step away from tennis and spend more time with his family. It allowed him to be present as his children grew up.In other words, Agassi may have missed parts of his own childhood, but later he had the opportunity to sit beside his children and watch them experience theirs. For him, that became a kind of second chance.Fatherhood gave Andre Agassi a different way of looking at his past. When he watched Jaden and Jaz grow up, he could see the small moments of childhood from a parent’s point of view.He could watch them discover what they liked, make their own choices and develop personalities separate from their famous parents.Those moments were very different from the childhood Agassi had experienced.His early years were strongly connected to the tennis court. His father believed that constant practice and discipline were necessary if Andre Agassi was going to become a champion. That approach helped produce an incredible tennis career, but it also meant that Agassi’s childhood was far from ordinary.As a father, he wanted something different for his children.Instead of seeing childhood as preparation for a future career, Agassi wanted Jaden and Jaz to enjoy the years they were living through.That is one of the most important ideas behind his quote. He was not simply saying that he wanted to give his children more material things or better opportunities. He wanted to give them time.Time to grow.Time to explore.Time to make mistakes.Time to decide what they wanted for themselves.This became especially important because Agassi knew from personal experience how powerful parental expectations can be. He had spent years trying to become the player his father wanted him to be. As a parent, he had the chance to make sure his own children did not feel that same pressure.Steffi Graf’s role in the family’s story is important because she understood Agassi’s world better than almost anyone. Like her husband, Graf was introduced to tennis at a very young age and went on to become one of the greatest players in the history of the sport.Steffi Graf won 22 Grand Slam singles titles and spent years at the top of women’s tennis before retiring in 1999. Agassi and Graf later married and raised their two children, Jaden and Jaz.Together, they had something unusual in common: both parents knew exactly what it took to become a tennis champion, but they also knew the pressure that came with that journey.That understanding appears to have influenced the way they raised their children.Despite having two parents who were global tennis stars, Jaden and Jaz were not simply expected to follow the same path.Jaden developed a passion for baseball rather than choosing tennis as his main sport. Jaz has also been able to follow her own interests. Andre Agassi and Graf have supported their children without making their parents’ careers the center of their lives.That is particularly meaningful when viewed alongside Agassi’s quote.The couple had already achieved what many athletes spend their entire lives chasing. They did not need their children to continue that legacy for them.Instead, they could give their children something that both parents understood the value of: choice.Agassi has also spoken warmly about Graf and the role she plays in his life. Their shared experience in professional sports gave them an understanding of the demands and sacrifices that come with elite competition.For their family, giving their children the freedom to choose their own paths became more important than creating another generation of tennis champions.At its heart, Agassi’s quote is about turning his own difficult experiences into something positive for his children.He cannot go back and change the childhood he had. He cannot erase the years of training, pressure and expectations that came with becoming a tennis player.But he can choose what kind of childhood his own children experience.That is what makes the quote about much more than tennis.Many parents work hard because they want their children to have opportunities they did not have themselves. Agassi’s story takes that idea one step further. His goal was not simply to provide his children with a comfortable life. He wanted to be present for the experiences that make childhood special.His words also show that parenthood can change the way people understand their own past.The same childhood that once felt difficult to Agassi became part of what helped him understand his children better. His experiences taught him what pressure can feel like, which may have made him more aware of the importance of giving his own children freedom.And Steffi Graf was there beside him, bringing her own experience as a former champion and a parent.Together, Agassi and Graf chose not to make their children’s lives about living up to their parents’ names. They allowed Jaden and Jaz to build identities of their own.That may be the most powerful part of Agassi’s words.He spent his childhood becoming a tennis champion. But when he became a father, he did not want his children to spend their childhood becoming something for him.He wanted to watch them simply be children.So, when Agassi says, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” he is not only talking about sacrifice. He is talking about perspective, presence and love.He gave years of his life to tennis. Those years helped him become a champion and eventually gave him the freedom to step back and focus on his family.For Agassi, one of the greatest rewards was not another trophy or achievement. It was being able to watch his children grow up on their own terms, with Graf by his side.That is what makes his quote so relatable. Parenthood does not allow us to rewrite our own childhoods, but it can give us the chance to create a different childhood for the next generation.
Article Summary: Tennis legend andre agassi said he gave up his childhood to have his children's childhood. The quote is closely connected to agassi's own experience growing up. Agassi grew up in a world where tennis was not simply a sport but a major part of his everyday life. Andre agassi and steffi graf have two children, jaden and jaz.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "I’m happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough.I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubius’ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.

Why a basketball game is the first place you will see this

Nvidia is switching on DLSS 5 on September 3 at 9pm Pacific Time, and the first game to use it is NBA 2K27. The feature works on every GeForce RTX 50 Series desktop and laptop GPU, and on GeForce NOW Ultimate, where sessions run on cloud rigs powered by RTX 5080 cards. A new Game Ready Driver lands the same night, and without it the toggle stays hidden.What DLSS 5 does is different from what the last few versions did. Super Resolution and Multi Frame Generation were about speed, reconstructing or multiplying pixels so frame rates climbed. 3D-Guided Neural Rendering instead puts back the detail studios normally strip out to stay real-time. It reads the engine's finished frame along with its motion vectors, then adds light scattering under skin, transmission through hair and foliage, tighter contact shadows and richer global illumination. Facial geometry and proportions stay exactly as the artists built them.Visual Concepts scans real athletes, so faces are the hardest thing to touch without breaking. On Cade Cunningham, arena lighting now warms the skin properly and shadows sit closer along the jersey collar. Tyrese Haliburton picks up cleaner shadow definition under the nose and across his compression sleeve. Senior producer Peter Kavic said the technology brought "a real jump to photorealism across the game".Developers get model choices plus Structure and Tone Intensity sliders, and semantic masking so the effect can be pushed on environments while characters are left alone. Integration runs through Nvidia Streamline or an Unreal Engine 5 plugin. For players it is one on-off switch, with F9 flipping it mid-game.Performance holds up. At 4K Ultra with ray tracing, an RTX 5090 reaches up to 370fps. At 1440p the RTX 5070 manages 260fps. Nvidia says it cut the cost fivefold in six months, from two 5090s to one card, with more optimisation due in the fall.
